staking_entity: Staked AAVE (stkAAVE) Safety Module staking contract
primary_gov_unit: Per-address on-chain balance snapshot: a holder's own AAVE + stkAAVE + aAAVE balances (plus delegations received), summed by the Aave GovernancePowerStrategy at the proposal snapshot block. stkAAVE is a snapshot-enabled ERC20 with its own per-holder governance-power and delegation accounting; it is the staked token itself that carries voting power to its individual holder, not a contract-level bloc. Off-chain Snapshot is non-binding pre-vote; binding votes are on-chain over these per-address balances.
staked_tokens_vote_detail: stkAAVE retains full governance voting power. Aave official docs: "AAVE, stkAAVE (AAVE staked in protocol safety module), and aAAVE token holders receive governance powers proportional to the sum of their balances on Ethereum mainnet." stkAAVE is described as "optimized for its usage as voting asset on Aave Governance v3."
voting_mechanism_detail: DISPERSED / per-staker. Verified at the contract level: GovernanceStrategy._getPowerByTypeAt computes power as IGovernancePowerDelegationToken(AAVE).getPowerAtBlock(user, blockNumber, powerType) + IGovernancePowerDelegationToken(STK_AAVE).getPowerAtBlock(user, blockNumber, powerType) for the SAME user address. The stkAAVE token (bgd-labs aave-stk-gov-v3) carries the same per-holder snapshot + delegation properties as the AAVE token. The Safety Module staking contract does NOT aggregate and cast a single bloc vote; each individual staker votes (or individually delegates) their own stkAAVE balance. The staking contract functions as a custody/wrapper layer for governance purposes.
insider_staking_risk_detail: LOW. stkAAVE is a permissionless pool (any AAVE holder can stake) and AAVE is ~95% circulating; genesis allocation went to LEND-to-AAVE migration (81.25%) and the governance-controlled Ecosystem Reserve (18.75%), with no public per-address evidence that team/foundation/investor tokens are specifically concentrated inside the Safety Module. Critically, because governance power is computed at the individual staker's address (not at the stkAAVE contract address), excluding the stkAAVE contract from the HHI does NOT hide any insider: an insider who stakes still appears in the HHI as their own holder row carrying their AAVE+stkAAVE balance. The reviewer's "insider tokens hidden in staking" concern is therefore structurally mitigated for AAVE, the governance unit the HHI should count is the staker's own address, which is directly visible.
reasoning: The reviewer's test is whether the staking contract disperses voting to individual stakers (custody -> exclude) or retains and casts votes as a bloc (concentration -> keep in HHI). For AAVE: (1) stkAAVE retains voting power (confirmed by Aave docs); but (2) that power is dispersed per-staker, verified directly in GovernanceStrategy/GovernancePowerStrategy contract code, which reads per-address balances from both the AAVE and stkAAVE tokens and sums them for that same user. There is no operator, validator, or contract-level aggregator that casts the staked AAVE as a single bloc. (3) The governance-voting unit is the holder's own balance snapshot (AAVE + stkAAVE + aAAVE + delegations) at the proposal block, on-chain binding; Snapshot off-chain is non-binding. (4) Because power attaches to the individual staker address rather than the contract, excluding the stkAAVE Safety Module contract address from the HHI does not mask insider concentration; insiders surface at their own wallets. Therefore PCA-excluding the stkAAVE contract address is correct: it is a custody/dispersed structure, not a concentration point. Note for the HHI builder: the correct unit is the individual staker address (AAVE + its stkAAVE balance combined per the additive strategy), and stkAAVE balances should be attributed back to / co-counted with the underlying holder so that a holder splitting across raw AAVE and stkAAVE is not under-counted. The single risk to monitor is delegation: if many small stakers delegate to one recipient, concentration would appear at the delegate address (visible on-chain via getPowerCurrent), not at the staking contract, so the exclusion remains correct and the delegate-level concentration is a separate, directly-measurable axis.

staking_entity: veCRV locker (vote-escrowed CRV) — Curve DAO VotingEscrow contract at 0x5f3b5DfEb7B28CDbD7FAba78963EE202a494e2A2
primary_gov_unit: veCRV balance (non-transferable, time-decayed vote-escrowed CRV) read per-address by the modified Aragon Voting App for onchain DAO proposals, and by the GaugeController for gauge-weight votes. Not raw CRV token balance; not delegated in the base protocol.
reasoning:
1) Do staked/locked tokens retain governance voting power? YES. Locking CRV mints veCRV, and veCRV is the sole governance unit in Curve. veCRV holders vote on all onchain Aragon DAO proposals (ownership votes: 30% quorum / 51% pass; parameter votes: 15% quorum / 30% pass; proposal creation gated at 2,500 veCRV) and direct CRV emissions via GaugeController gauge-weight votes. So this is NOT a no-governance staking contract; it is THE governance instrument.

2) Dispersed or bloc? DISPERSED. Curve uses a modified Aragon Voting App where the standard 1-token-1-vote is replaced by per-address time-weighted veCRV balance. Each locker address casts its own vote weighted by its own individual veCRV balance (which decays linearly to unlock). The VotingEscrow contract is a single contract that holds all the underlying locked CRV, but internally it maps locks per user and does NOT itself cast an aggregate vote; there is no operator/validator/contract voting the bloc on lockers' behalf. (Layered wrappers like Convex/vlCVX aggregate voting power as a separate bloc, but those are distinct protocol-owned addresses, not the native veCRV locker.)

3) Governance-voting unit: per-address veCRV balance (time- and amount-weighted, non-transferable), read by the Aragon Voting App / GaugeController. Critically, this is NOT the raw CRV ERC-20 balance. The VotingEscrow contract appears in a raw-CRV holder snapshot as one enormous single holder, but governance is exercised at the per-locker veCRV layer.

4) Insider tokens locked here? HIGHLY PLAUSIBLE / confirmed in part. 30% of CRV supply went to team + early investors (vested through Aug 2024), and founder Michael Egorov has publicly stated he keeps a large amount of CRV locked as veCRV. Because there is ONE VotingEscrow contract holding ALL locked CRV, any insider veCRV position lives inside that single contract address.

PCA verdict -> needs_author_decision. The reviewer's two concerns split in opposite directions here:
(a) Bloc-voting test: the veCRV locker FAILS to be a bloc-voting concentration point — voting is genuinely dispersed per locker, the contract is custody, not a voting actor. On that test alone, excluding the locker-as-single-holder from a raw-CRV HHI is defensible (treating the contract address as one $-billion governance actor would be WRONG).
(b) Insider-hiding test + unit mismatch: BUT excluding the whole veCRV contract from a raw-CRV-balance HHI hides insider veCRV concentration (founder + team/investor locks) that genuinely IS concentrated governance power. The deeper problem is that raw CRV balance is the WRONG governance unit for Curve: governance runs on per-address veCRV, so the HHI should be built over the veCRV (per-locker) distribution, not over raw CRV with the locker excluded as custody. If the study measures raw CRV balances and excludes the locker, it simultaneously (correctly) avoids the one-giant-holder artifact AND (incorrectly) deletes the most concentration-relevant population (the lockers, including insiders) from the index.

Recommendation requiring author decision: do not simply 'exclude veCRV as a PCA.' Instead, recompute the governance HHI over the per-address veCRV distribution (the actual voting unit), which both removes the contract-as-single-actor artifact AND surfaces insider concentration inside the locker. Excluding the locker is only 'correct' if the HHI is explicitly a raw-token-custody index rather than a governance-power index; for a governance-concentration study, that exclusion is materially under-inclusive of the real governance distribution.

staking_entity: veFXS (vote-escrowed FXS), contract 0xc8418aF6358FFddA74e09Ca9CC3Fe03Ca6aDC5b0 on Ethereum mainnet (plus Fraxtal-chain veFXS)
reasoning:
veFXS is NOT mere custody and DOES retain governance voting power: veFXS holders control gauge weights, protocol parameters, strategic decisions, and per the docs have "the final say over everything in the protocol," plus they receive the protocol's primary cash-flow distribution. So the "no governance role" path to exclusion does not apply.

The voting model is DISPERSED, not bloc. veFXS is described as "an account based point system," is non-transferable, and "your veFXS balance is equal to your voting power." The Snapshot strategy computes voting power via balanceOf(address) on the veFXS contract for each voting address; each locker votes its OWN veFXS balance. The veFXS contract / staking system does not cast a single aggregate bloc vote, and there is no operator/validator that votes the pooled position. Delegation exists but is holder-directed (a locker may delegate to whomever they choose), which does not make the contract itself a concentration point. This satisfies the reviewer's "disperses voting to individual stakers" condition for legitimate PCA exclusion.

Therefore the verdict is exclusion_correct WITH a load-bearing caveat the author must heed: because the governance-voting unit is the per-address veFXS balance and NOT the veFXS contract's aggregate balance, the on-chain veFXS contract address (which holds the pooled locked FXS) is correctly excluded from an HHI built over token-holder addresses ONLY IF the study's HHI is intended to measure the distribution of liquid/transferable FXS holdings, OR if the study re-attributes the locked stake to individual locker addresses. If the study merely DELETES the veFXS contract's large aggregate balance from a raw-FXS-balance HHI without re-attributing that stake to the underlying lockers, it would understate governance concentration by hiding exactly the actor distribution that actually votes. The correct governance-concentration HHI is over individual veFXS locker addresses (their balanceOf at the snapshot block), not over raw FXS balances minus the contract. The reviewer's bloc-voting concern (operator votes the aggregate) does NOT apply to veFXS, so the exclusion is not "questionable_should_be_in_HHI" on bloc grounds.

Insider-staking risk is HIGH. FXS distribution allocated 20% to Team/Founders/Early Members, 12% to Accredited Private Investors, 3% to Strategic Advisors, and 5% to Project Treasury. veFXS is the protocol's primary cash-flow AND governance mechanism, giving insiders strong incentive to lock; the veFXS/Snapshot strategy infrastructure was authored by the founding team (FortisFortuna / Sam Kazemian). It is highly plausible that team/treasury/investor FXS is locked as veFXS. If the audited study excludes the veFXS contract as a single PCA without re-attributing locked balances to individual lockers, insider veFXS positions would be invisible to the holder-concentration count, which is precisely the second risk the reviewer raised. So while the bridge/CEX-style PCA exclusion of the contract address is mechanically correct, the author should confirm the HHI is computed over per-locker veFXS balances (where insider lockers appear as their own concentrated addresses) rather than over a raw-FXS-balance set with the contract simply removed.

staking_entity: Staked ENA (sENA) staking/lock contract, governance space ethenagovernance.eth on Snapshot
primary_gov_unit: Snapshot off-chain, balance-weighted vote. The space (ethenagovernance.eth) counts ENA and sENA balances; sENA carries voting power with a lock-duration multiplier (longer lock = higher weight). Not a single on-chain Tally vote by the contract; not a delegate-to-operator model. Each address signs its own vote.
reasoning:
Two axes, splitting opposite ways, which is why this is needs_author_decision rather than a clean exclusion_correct or exclusion_questionable.

AXIS 1 (the reviewer's bloc-vs-dispersed test) -> supports exclusion. sENA retains governance voting power (Ethena docs: "sENA holders will be able to vote directly on ENA tokenomics proposals and any proposals concerning ENA specifically"), so this is NOT a no-governance-role custody contract like some staking. However, voting is conducted on Snapshot (off-chain) in the space ethenagovernance.eth, where voting power is balance/lock-weighted and EACH address signs its own vote. There is no operator, validator, or the sENA contract itself casting one aggregate bloc vote on behalf of all stakers. By construction the sENA contract is custody for governance purposes: votes disperse to individual stakers/lockers. On a pure bloc-voting test the exclusion is defensible (dispersed_per_staker), so it is NOT a clear exclusion_questionable_should_be_in_HHI on the operator-bloc theory.

AXIS 2 (the reviewer's insider-hidden-in-staking concern) -> challenges exclusion, and is the load-bearing reason for needs_author_decision. There is a DOCUMENTED October 2024 episode: Ethena moved ~180,000,000 ENA (reported as ~25% of the then-sENA staking supply) from foundation-related wallets (six wallets via Coinbase Prime) into sENA to farm Season 3 sats. Ethena's defense was that these were UNLOCKED FOUNDATION tokens, not locked team/investor tokens, and that locked team/investor tokens are not staked. But (a) Foundation is ~15% of supply and Core Contributors ~30% / Investors ~25%, so a foundation-controlled position of this size inside sENA is a genuine concentrated, governance-ELIGIBLE actor (sENA votes), and (b) the community disputed the transparency, given Ethena's history of mid-stream rule changes. If the PCA rule blanket-excludes the entire sENA contract from the HHI, it deletes this large foundation-controlled, vote-bearing bloc from the concentration measure. That is precisely the "insider tokens hidden in staking" failure the reviewer flagged. The HHI-renormalization-under-exclusion hazard compounds it: naive whole-contract exclusion both hides the insider bloc and renormalizes the remaining shares.

NET: The sENA contract is not a single bloc voter (axis 1 clean), but it is a custody wrapper that demonstrably holds a large foundation/insider position which DOES carry Snapshot voting power (axis 2 not clean). Wholesale exclusion is therefore not obviously correct: the author must decide whether to (a) keep the sENA contract excluded but separately attribute identifiable foundation/insider sENA balances back into the insider count / HHI, or (b) treat sENA as a custody pass-through and attribute each large staker's underlying balance to that staker (which would re-capture the foundation bloc). Either way the foundation/insider portion should not vanish. Recommend author decision plus an attempt to identify the six foundation-related sENA-staking wallets (out of scope for web-only tools; would need on-chain/Nansen, which were prohibited here).

CAVEAT: I could not load the live ethenagovernance.eth Snapshot strategy JSON via WebFetch to read the exact strategy name(s) and whether the strategy counts sENA at the wallet level vs the contract level; docs and secondary sources consistently describe per-holder Snapshot voting with a lock multiplier, which is dispersed by construction. If the author wants belt-and-suspenders confirmation, pull the space strategies from the Snapshot API/UI directly.

primary_gov_unit: Snapshot off-chain voting using sETHFI (staked ETHFI) vote-power balances, plus raw unstaked ETHFI; sETHFI is an OpenZeppelin ERC20Votes token with per-account checkpoints and optional per-staker delegation. Quorum 1M ETHFI, 4-day window.
reasoning:
1) RETAIN VOTING: Yes. Staked ETHFI retains governance power. ether.fi docs: "Yes! You can vote on ether.fi DAO proposals through Snapshot" with staked ETHFI. The DAO Staking Contract Implementation proposal states "Users will be able to vote with their staked tokens, enhancing decentralized governance" (and non-staked ETHFI can still vote too). This is NOT a no-governance-role stake (unlike pure points/reward stakes).

2) DISPERSED vs BLOC: DISPERSED per-staker. The sETHFI contract (Staked ETHFI, 0x86b5780b...9518c0161) is a verified OpenZeppelin ERC20Votes token: it maintains per-account vote checkpoints (Checkpoints library), exposes delegate()/delegateBySig()/getVotes()/getPastVotes(), and emits DelegateChanged/DelegateVotesChanged. Vote power is tracked per holder, and each staker votes (or delegates) its own sETHFI balance. The contract holds 7,105 holders' stakes (~85.4M sETHFI) but does NOT cast a single aggregate vote; there is no operator/validator voting the bloc. Staking re-routes delegation from Agora to the staking contract's per-account delegation, i.e. it is custody with vote pass-through, not bloc aggregation. 4) INSIDER-STAKING RISK: MEDIUM. ETHFI is insider-heavy (Core Contributors 21.47%, Investors 33.74%, Treasury 21.62% = ~77% of 1B supply) under 1yr cliff + 2-3yr linear vesting. The public staking contract is permissionless, so insiders whose tokens have unlocked could stake into sETHFI, which would commingle them with 7,105 holders and could partially obscure an insider address in a top-holder/PCA scan. Mitigants that cap the risk at medium (not high): vested/locked insider tranches sit in separate vesting contracts under cliffs (not in the staking contract); and because sETHFI vote power is per-account-checkpointed rather than aggregated, an insider's staked position remains an individually attributable voting unit rather than being hidden behind a single bloc voter. So excluding the staking contract from the HHI does not, by itself, conceal a concentrated insider bloc, though it could conceal a large individual insider staker if the HHI is built on holder addresses without unwinding sETHFI to underlying stakers.

VERDICT: exclusion_correct. The sETHFI staking contract is custody that disperses voting per staker (ERC20Votes per-account + delegation, Snapshot), not a single concentrated governance actor, so PCA exclusion from the HHI is justified. GnosisDAO governance is Snapshot off-chain, and via GIP-28 -> GIP-44 -> GIP-140 it explicitly extends voting power to GNO in invested/staked/locked positions: LGNO, sGNO/osGNO, and deposit/validator GNO. So staked/locked GNO unambiguously retains governance voting power (answer to Q1: yes).

LGNO specifically is a non-transferable 1:1 lock-claim token issued PER DEPOSITOR by the Gnosis token-lock contract (the vCOW / Safe-airdrop lock program at lock.gnosis.io), ~219K supply across ~409 holders. The residual risk: if the study's HHI is built on RAW on-chain top-holder balances (where GNO parked in the LGNO/staking contract is attributed to the contract address and then PCA-excluded) rather than on the governance strategy's resolved per-holder voting weights, then excluding the contract could mask whichever holders (including any insiders) locked there. GNO has a small supply (3M max, ~2.6M circulating), which amplifies any single locked insider block. Recommend the author note that the exclusion is correct for the governance-voting-unit HHI, but if the HHI is computed on raw balances the LGNO/staking-contract balance should be decomposed to underlying lockers (per the same strategy GnosisDAO uses) before exclusion, to avoid hiding insider concentration.

Voting power is computed from each address's own self-staked/delegated POL (read from its ValidatorShare/StakeManager position) and attributed back to the individual staker, who may delegate part or all to multiple delegates. voting_mechanism_detail: POL has two coexisting governance regimes. For PIP/System-contract governance (the public token-holder governance pillar relevant to a holder-concentration HHI), voting is DISPERSED per staker: the StakeManagerProxy/ValidatorShare contracts are custody/accounting, and the `polygon-self-staked-pol` Snapshot strategy attributes each staker's staked balance back to that staker's own address. For Heimdall consensus-layer governance, voting is BLOC: only validators vote, weighted by validating stake, and Heimdall does not support delegation. The contract-as-single-actor concentration concern is therefore weak for the PIP pillar but real at the consensus layer.
staked_tokens_vote_detail: Staking (delegating POL to a PoS validator) is the PREREQUISITE for governance participation. governance.polygon.technology: community members must stake POL by delegating to a PoS validator before they can vote or delegate voting power. So staked/locked POL is not voting-inert; it is the canonical governance unit.
insider_staking_detail: High risk that insider tokens are hidden in this contract. Roughly 3.6 billion POL is locked in validator staking contracts (the stated rationale for the sPOL liquid-staking-token launch was to unlock 3.6B+ POL locked in validator staking). Validator incentives are ~8.98% of the 10B supply and the community treasury ~8.98%; Polygon-Labs/foundation-operated validators and treasury-staked positions are a plausible channel for team/foundation/investor allocations to sit inside StakeManagerProxy. Excluding the StakeManager aggregate from the top-holder set therefore risks removing a large insider-allocation channel from the visible holder count, INDEPENDENT of the dispersed-vs-bloc voting question.
reasoning: PCA verdict is needs_author_decision, not a clean exclusion_correct, for two independent reasons. (1) Voting-concentration axis is mixed: for the public PIP/System-contract governance pillar the staked balance disperses back to individual stakers via the `polygon-self-staked-pol` Snapshot strategy (so the contract is custody, not a single bloc actor, supporting exclusion), but a genuine BLOC regime exists at the Heimdall consensus layer where validators vote aggregated stake and delegators have no vote. Which pillar the study's HHI is meant to capture determines whether exclusion is correct. (2) Insider-hiding axis is the stronger concern and is orthogonal to dispersion: ~3.6B POL sits locked in validator staking contracts, and foundation/Labs/treasury validator positions could conceal insider concentration; excluding the whole StakeManager aggregate hides that regardless of how votes disperse. The reviewer's concern is partially answered (public-pillar votes do disperse) but not fully neutralized (consensus-layer bloc voting + insider-token concealment remain). Author should decide: (a) which governance regime the HHI targets, and (b) whether to net out / separately account for foundation/treasury/Labs-validator staked positions before excluding the StakeManager aggregate. primary_gov_unit: Snapshot off-chain governance using the custom "iotex-staked-balance" strategy: each voting address's OWN staked IOTX balance (1 IOTX = 1 vote) plus stake-duration bonus votes. Not raw token balance, not the delegate's aggregate. Governance weight exists ONLY for staked IOTX; unstaked balances carry no IIP-voting weight.
staking_entity: IoTeX SystemStaking contract (native on-chain staking pool that issues per-staker NFT "bucket" positions; the pool address holds all staked IOTX in aggregate)
reasoning:
Two distinct "voting" systems must not be conflated. (1) Roll-DPoS CONSENSUS delegation: stakers vote IOTX to delegates who produce blocks; this is aggregated by delegate, but it governs block production, not protocol governance. (2) Protocol GOVERNANCE (IIP) voting: conducted off-chain on Snapshot (gov.iotex.io) with the custom "iotex-staked-balance" strategy. For (2), voting is DISPERSED per-staker: each staker connects their own wallet and votes their own staked balance ("the number of votes you have is based on the amount of IOTX YOU have staked"). The Snapshot strategy reads per-address staked IOTX + duration bonus, NOT the delegate's total. Community evidence confirms delegates do NOT auto-cast governance votes for IOTX staked to them (a staker complained the delegate did not vote on his behalf, so he had to vote himself). The SystemStaking contract is custody/pooling: each staker owns an NFT bucket, controls its lock, can switch delegate, and unstakes independently. So the contract is NOT a single concentrated governance actor casting a bloc IIP vote, and it is NOT bloc-voting concentration that belongs in the HHI as one actor.

HOWEVER, wholesale exclusion of the contract ADDRESS from a GOVERNANCE-concentration HHI is methodologically problematic, because governance weight lives ENTIRELY inside staked IOTX. The SystemStaking contract pools ALL staked IOTX under one on-chain address; an HHI computed over raw top-holder token balances that simply drops that one address nets out the entire governance-active supply and hides whatever insider positions are locked inside it. The correct governance unit is the per-staker bucket (the same unit the Snapshot vote uses), so the right treatment is to DECOMPOSE the contract into per-owner bucket balances and run the HHI over those, not to exclude the contract wholesale. Whether the study did that decomposition vs. a blanket address-level exclusion is an author construction decision -> needs_author_decision.

Insider-staking risk is HIGH: governance weight = staked IOTX, and to earn rewards or qualify as a delegate, insider-adjacent allocations are economically motivated to be staked (hence sitting inside the contract). IoTeX has very large insider/treasury pools that plausibly stake: the original 1.2B IOTX (12% of supply) staking-rewards allocation; 500M+ IOTX repurposed into the Marshall DAO treasury (community-voted Q1 2024); and every delegate self-staking >=1.2M IOTX (delegates need 1.2M self-stake + 2M total votes). If any of these are inside the SystemStaking pool, a blanket exclusion of the contract hides material insider governance concentration. Limitation: I could not confirm via public docs the exact current breakdown of which foundation/team/treasury wallets are actively staked inside the contract (on-chain holder decomposition / Nansen-style labeling would be needed and is out of scope per instructions), so the risk is assessed as high-likelihood rather than verified.

staking_entity: Anyone Protocol relay-staking / lock-staking (per-relay-fingerprint lock contract) plus the on-chain governance contract 0x0d9a1ca7Bc756AE009672Db626CdE3c9BEF583EF (votesOf), with off-chain tallying on the daoforanyone.eth Snapshot space
primary_gov_unit: Snapshot off-chain voting whose weight is read from each address's own on-chain lock-staked/double-staked position via votesOf(address). The governance unit is the per-address lock-staked (LS) position, quadratically weighted by stake size and lock duration (VP = sqrt(Cx * M), M = 1 + 0.0035*D^2, multiplier capped at 290). It is NOT the raw ERC-20 balance and NOT a delegated aggregate; governance mode is opt-in and one-way per wallet.
reasoning: Governance is LIVE on Snapshot (space "DAO for ANyONe", daoforanyone.eth, Ethereum mainnet). The space's voting strategy is a contract-call to votesOf(address) on governance contract 0x0d9a1ca7Bc756AE009672Db626CdE3c9BEF583EF (distinct from the ERC-20 0xfeac2eae96899709a43e252b6b92971d32f9c0f9). votesOf is a per-address lookup: each voter's power is derived from THEIR OWN lock-staked/double-staked position, quadratically weighted (VP = sqrt(Cx * M); M = 1 + 0.0035*D^2; cap 290). Governance mode is opt-in and one-way per wallet (enabled at dashboard.anyone.io; extends unstake 7->30 days). This is dispersed voting: each staker votes their own share. There is NO single contract/operator/validator that casts the aggregate as a bloc. On custody, the staking lock is tracked per relay fingerprint (individual custody, NOT a pooled network balance): 100 ANYONE, 180-day minimum, fingerprint-specific; the lock is effectively a custody/eligibility deposit tied to relay operation. Under the reviewer's own test (PCA-exclude only if the contract disperses voting to individual stakers), exclusion is CORRECT: the lock contract is mere per-operator custody and governance weight resolves to the individual staker, not the contract. Insider-staking risk is LOW: the relay lock is capped at 100 ANYONE per fingerprint (square-root taper on overstake), so it cannot warehouse large team/foundation/investor allocations; those sit in vesting/treasury wallets (~10-15% team/early-contributor with multi-year vesting; ~25% in-contract/treasury) that are separate from the relay-lock contract, and any such wallet that opts into governance votes only its OWN votesOf position rather than being aggregated into a single hidden bloc. Caveat: one earlier doc surface framed governance as a future centralized-to-DAO transition; the live Snapshot space config and the tokenomics docs (governance mode opt-in, votesOf strategy) supersede that as the current on-chain ground truth. No Nansen or write tools used; web/fetch only.

primary_gov_unit: Snapshot off-chain voting (space maple.eth) reading each voter's own ERC-20 wallet balance via two erc20-balance-of strategies: the staked receipt token stSYRUP (0xc7E8b36E0766D9B04c93De68A9D47dD11f260B45) plus raw SYRUP (0x643C4E15d7d62Ad0aBeC4a9BD4b001aA3Ef52d66), summed 1:1, on Ethereum mainnet. The staked/receipt token (held in the staker's own wallet) is itself the governance-voting unit, not the staking-contract address; no delegation configured.
staking_entity: stSYRUP staked-SYRUP vault (receipt/vault token; the post-migration successor to xMPL). Underlying SYRUP pooled in the staking contract; appreciating receipt token stSYRUP held in each staker's wallet. Contract 0xc7E8b36E0766D9B04c93De68A9D47dD11f260B45.
reasoning: Staked tokens RETAIN governance voting power: stSYRUP was made the sole governance token under MIP-012, and per MIP-019 (Oct 2025) both SYRUP and stSYRUP holders can vote. (Legacy MPL/xMPL no longer carry governance rights; SYRUP/stSYRUP are the sole governance tokens post-migration.) Voting is DISPERSED per staker, not a bloc: the maple.eth Snapshot space (confirmed via hub.snapshot.org/api/spaces/maple.eth) uses two erc20-balance-of strategies over stSYRUP and SYRUP with no delegation. erc20-balance-of returns each voter's OWN wallet balance. stSYRUP is an appreciating receipt/vault token (exchange-rate style; per docs the amount of stSYRUP received decreases over time as it appreciates) held in each staker's own wallet, so the staking contract pools the underlying SYRUP but the receipt token in individual wallets carries the vote. No contract, operator, or validator casts an aggregate bloc vote. PCA EXCLUSION CORRECT: the staking-contract address is mere custody of the underlying SYRUP and is not a governance-concentration point; the vote rides on per-wallet stSYRUP receipt-token balances, so excluding the staking-contract address from the HHI does not drop a bloc voter. INSIDER-STAKING RISK is LOW in the specific sense the reviewer worried about (insider tokens hidden inside an excluded contract address): even if team/investor/treasury SYRUP is staked, their stSYRUP receipt tokens sit in individual insider wallets and vote individually via erc20-balance-of, so insider concentration surfaces at the per-wallet level rather than being masked by the contract address. Caveat for the author: Maple insider allocations are large (Seed Investors ~21.2%, Team & Advisors ~20.4%, Treasury ~30%), and MIP-019 showed 30% of voting power from a single address among only 26 voting wallets, so governance is concentrated; but that concentration would (and should) appear in the individual top-holder/voter wallets the HHI counts, not be hidden by the PCA-excluded staking contract. The exclusion of the stSYRUP staking-contract address itself is methodologically sound.

staking_entity: GEOD Staking Pool (GEODNET) - the SuperHex staking contract at 0x682ba846eed9934cc89ed89a350ea98781256b6f, plus the conflated "Locked GEOD" veNFT category that holds team/investor allocations
primary_gov_unit: veNFT (voting-escrow "Voting NFT" power score), not raw GEOD balance. Total veNFT = Location NFT votes + Staked GEOD votes + Locked GEOD votes. Voting runs on GEODNET's own app-based governance portal (vote.geodnet.com), not standard Snapshot-offchain or a Tally on-chain Governor; users connect their own MetaMask and their veNFT is auto-calculated from their own Location NFTs / staked GEOD / locked GEOD.
reasoning:
GEODNET governance does NOT disenfranchise staked/locked tokens, so the "mere custody, no governance role" rationale for PCA exclusion fails on its face. The voting unit is the veNFT, computed from three sources, two of which are the staking/locking entity in question: Staked GEODs (SuperHex community stakers) and Locked GEODs (team/investors held as "foundation members"). Tokenomics: team 25% + investors 25% = 50% of the 1B supply, on multi-year vesting/lock, and the docs state team/investor locked GEOD is "also allocated veNFT governance tokens." So insider tokens are unambiguously locked inside the locking layer that the study excludes, and they retain governance power. Insider-staking-risk = high.

The dispersed-vs-bloc question splits into two sub-entities that the single "GEOD Staking Pool" label conflates:

(1) SuperHex community staking contract (0x682ba846eed9934cc89ed89a350ea98781256b6f): tokens sit in a shared contract, but each staker controls and redeems their own position via Console+MetaMask, and the personal-account-center docs show each user votes their own auto-calculated veNFT through their own MetaMask wallet. This sub-entity is DISPERSED per-staker custody, and for it exclusion is defensible.

(2) Locked GEOD (team/investors/foundation): the docs explicitly say these holders have "locked their GEOD tokens in either a smart contract or custodian account," cannot connect via MetaMask, and therefore "delegate their veNFT to another wallet address," and "will be contacted individually to set up a delegated veNFT wallet." That is delegation of insider voting power, plausibly to a foundation-coordinated bloc wallet. This sub-entity carries genuine concentration and BLOC-voting risk, and excluding it would hide ~50%-of-allocation insider concentration plus the largest single coordinated governance actor.

Because the protocol's named "GEOD Staking Pool" entity bundles (a) a legitimately-excludable dispersed community staking layer with (b) an insider locked-token layer that retains delegated, plausibly-bloc veNFT voting power, this is not cleanly exclusion_correct nor cleanly exclusion_questionable. It requires the author to decide whether to (i) split the entity and keep only the dispersed community-staking portion excluded while pulling the team/investor locked veNFT back INTO the HHI (or treating it as a distinct insider concentration node), or (ii) treat the whole thing as a concentration point. Either way, blanket exclusion of the entire entity is unsafe given the explicit team+investor locked-veNFT-with-delegation evidence. Overall voting_mechanism is marked unclear because the platform is a bespoke veNFT portal whose actual vote-execution path (per-user signature vs delegated aggregate for the locked tranche) differs by tranche and is not fully documented; the documented delegation path for insiders is the bloc-risk signal.

primary_gov_unit: Bonded/staked LPT in the BondingManager, aggregated by default to the orchestrator/transcoder address (the operator votes the sum of self-stake + delegated stake). Voting power is read from on-chain stake checkpoints (LIP-16 era: pendingStake / Transcoder.totalStake via off-chain indexed tally; LIP-91 Delta treasury era: BondingVotes getVotes checkpoints feeding an OpenZeppelin Governor on Arbitrum L2). Not raw wallet token balance, not a separate ve-token, not Snapshot-offchain.
staking_entity: Livepeer LPT staking (bonding/transcoder delegation) — BondingManager; orchestrators/transcoders vote delegated stake
reasoning:
Staked LPT DOES retain governance power, and the default voting unit is the orchestrator/transcoder, who casts the full weight of its delegated stake (self-stake plus all delegators bonded to it) unless a delegator actively votes to override. This is bloc-by-default with opt-out dispersion, NOT dispersed-per-staker custody.

Mechanism evidence across both governance eras:
- LIP-16 polling (original): orchestrator vote weight = its total stake; a delegator who votes independently has their stake added to the orchestrator's nonVoteStake and subtracted from the orchestrator's tally ('voteStake - nonVoteStake'). The Livepeer Governance wiki states it directly: 'By default transcoder's votes carry the full weight of their delegated stake, however bonded nodes can change their own vote, taking their stake with them if they wish.'
- LIP-91 / Delta on-chain treasury Governor (current): the counting module is literally named GovernorCountingOverridable with explicit 'support for delegators to override their delegates (transcoders) vote.' Voting power is sourced from BondingVotes/getVotes checkpoints of bonded stake. Default = orchestrator aggregates delegated voting power; override only on opt-out.

Because the default is aggregate bloc-voting by the operator (the orchestrator address concentrates many delegators' stake), the BondingManager / staking layer is a genuine governance concentration point, not mere custody that disperses to individual stakers. The reviewer's concern applies: blanket PCA-excluding the staking/bonding contract removes a real bloc-voting actor from the HHI. The correct treatment is to attribute stake to the orchestrator addresses (concentration points) and keep them IN the HHI, rather than excluding the BondingManager wholesale.

Insider-staking risk is MEDIUM: founders/early team hold 12.35% and long-term endowment 5%; Livepeer Inc. and the Livepeer Foundation operate their own orchestrator nodes, which requires self-delegating/bonding LPT through the same BondingManager. Insider allocations bonded as self-stake would be hidden inside any contract-level exclusion, masking insider concentration. Not rated HIGH only because public allocation/self-stake figures were not directly confirmed in this search; the structural pathway is clearly present.

Verdict: exclusion_questionable_should_be_in_HHI. Recommend re-attributing bonded stake to orchestrator addresses (and to insider self-stake addresses) and including those concentration points in the HHI, rather than excluding the BondingManager as a protocol-controlled custody address.
